questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose Frankfurt because it is a city where finance is a big part of the identity, and where the language was German so I could perfect my German.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I really enjoyed my experience in Frankfurt. It is a city that deserves much more attention. I really liked the university campus. The facilities, the professors, and the vibrant social life on campus were truly amazing and among the main reasons why my stay was so rewarding.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Goethe University was very helpful, so I never had any issues. Whenever there was anything I was unsure about, they had already informed me who to contact. They respond quickly, so I only have good words for the people at Goethe University.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Because I was well informed beforehand and they arranged everything, I didn’t have any issues upon arrival.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I was ready on Mobility Online as soon as Goethe University opened the application for student dorms. They have a few around the city, and I was lucky to get one. Be fast and ready with everything they need from you so you get one of the rooms. My experience was that people who didn’t get a dorm room spent a lot of energy at the beginning finding housing. Mine was super convenient. I lived 10 minutes away from campus by bike.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Don’t expect high quality rooms. It is simple living with the bare minimum, but that’s fine because you only sleep there. Living in one of the dorms also makes it much easier to make friends because you live together and share experiences. Overall, the dorm option through the university was both affordable and easy.

How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was very easy because they have documents for everything. Further, they host introduction meetings where they show exactly what to do.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You get access to their course portal. You find the courses you are interested in and you find the document with the exam dates. Then you need to plan so you don’t have two or more exams on the same day, and also make sure classes are not at the same time. You make your own weekly schedule based on the courses that fit with each other. After finding the courses that work for you, you simply fill out a form with the courses you want, your student ID, and sign it. Send it by email and they then confirm if you got the spot. If you find out you don’t want one of the courses, you just fill out a de-registration form. You can do this up until approx. two weeks before the exam but you need to check de-registration dates before you apply so you don’t end up in a bad situation.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: They help you a lot. You can write the administration or any German ESN student and they will help you. I asked German students before applying about the courses and their experiences to get some recommendations, and it helped me a lot.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was succesful. You can apply for more courses than you need. I applied for 8 courses, and after 2 weeks of class I deregistered from 3 that I didn’t like as much, so I ended up with 5.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Apply for more than you need, but remember to deregister from the ones you don’t take. And plan carefully around exam dates.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was very satisfied. I really loved that all the professors had work experience outside university and could use their experiences to make realistic cases and relate to theory in a fulfilling way. I was way more engaged and excited to go to class.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: For all courses you have to read a lot. But it is okay, because there is way more of a studying life compared to at Copenhagen University, and they had space for everyone. I could always find seating around campus and they have great libraries. I had five classes, where three of them were quite demanding, not only in regards to reading but also the level of difficulty in the exercises.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The style of teaching at Goethe University was much more to my liking. The culture was that everyone came prepared for class, which meant professors could engage students more actively. This led to better discussions, and students asked way more questions than what I am used to at UCPH.

From a practical point of view, lectures and classes were quite similar to UCPH, with professors using slides and exercises. However, some professors preferred a more traditional approach, teaching only with the blackboard and not providing any notes, so you had to make sure to write everything down yourself.

What I especially liked was that the professor-student relationship was more traditional and professional. I appreciated this atmosphere of mutual respect and professionalism, and it felt more like a university with high expectations for itself and a focus on maintaining a certain standard.

Another difference I noticed is that at Goethe University, the teaching stayed neutral in terms of politics.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Insurance and Finance: The professor teaches in a traditional way, using only the blackboard, and I really enjoyed his lectures. With his extensive experience from the insurance sector, all the theory made sense when he illustrated it with real-world examples. The pace and structure of the course were excellent, and if you, like me, are curious about the insurance industry, this course gives you a solid understanding.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very satisfied. At Goethe University they have way more focus on creating a good university environment with lots of different sport clubs, creative opportunities, language classes and organisations, events, music, competitions (both non-academic and academic), and way more collaboration with companies from the real world.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: All kinds.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Try a lot of them. Personally, I really enjoyed the language café and the different sport clubs.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Here are a few:
- Explore the city’s many opportunities and areas. I really liked Westend.
- The bars all over Sachsenhausen.
- Watch a Frankfurt football game.
- Explore the cities around Frankfurt. Because everyone has a Deutschland Ticket, every weekend there was a one-day trip to a city relatively close by. Examples: Marburg, Heidelberg, Mannheim, Würzburg, etc.
- I personally also went on longer trips with other exchange students, for example to Dortmund to watch a football match, Trier, Luxembourg, Cologne, etc.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found it quite easy because I already spoke German. Just be aware that it is good to be able to speak German because even though the university is very international and most speak English, your daily life in the city and at places like the supermarket or municipal offices is just easier when you speak German.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join student organisations, language cafés, and sports clubs. They are great ways to meet German students. Group projects in class are also a good opportunity to connect, so try to be active and engaged.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There wasn’t really anything that I found particularly challenging. Everything came quite naturally and the locals were super helpful. I would mention one thing, which the locals will also tell you: stay away from Hauptbahnhof.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The outgoing locals and other internationals. Because the city is very multicultural, my experience was also that you could speak with anyone.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Study regularly during the semester. The exam period is short, intense, and more stressful than at UCPH.

2. Don’t overthink the administrative side. Most things are arranged for you, and the process is easier than it looks. They are super helpful and there is always someone to contact.

3. Enjoy it while it lasts. The semester goes by quickly, so take the opportunities that come your way.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be quick with housing applications.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends I met and how much I enjoyed living in another country and speaking German.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The exam period. I had never been so stressed and tired at the same time, but it was manageable because I kept up with my studies during the semester - something the local students thankfully warn you about from the very beginning. And they don’t give you access to previous exams when you prepare, therefore it’s even more important to follow the lectures and do the exercises.

questions.answer: Yes
